deck:
Markets ended a volatile week with a strong Friday rebound, but the bigger picture was less encouraging. The S&P 500, Nasdaq, Dow, and Russell 2000 all finished the week lower as a surge in oil prices, persistent inflation, and rising Treasury yields pushed interest-rate risk back to the center of the market.

The S&P 500 finished Friday at 7,656.98, but still lost 0.8% for the week. The Nasdaq declined 0.7%, the Dow fell 1.6%, and the Russell 2000 dropped 2.4%.

The biggest change this week was in the bond and energy markets. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed to roughly 4.97%, approaching the psychologically important 5% level, while WTI crude finished at $100.05 per barrel and Brent at $104.61.

At the same time, August inflation data remained firm. CPI rose 3.4% year over year, while producer prices increased 5.4%. That combination has sharply increased expectations that the Federal Reserve could raise rates at its September 16 meeting.

The next several days could determine whether the market's recent rally can continue or whether higher rates and energy prices begin to create a larger valuation reset.

sections.heading: 1. Equities: Friday's Rally Could Not Save the Week
body:
Stocks finished Friday strongly after oil prices pulled back from their highs.

The S&P 500 gained about 0.9% Friday, the Nasdaq rose roughly 1%, and the Dow added about 1%.

Despite that rebound, all three indexes finished lower for the week.

The S&P 500 lost 0.8%, while the Nasdaq fell 0.7%. The Dow performed worse, declining 1.6%. Small-cap stocks showed even more weakness, with the Russell 2000 falling 2.4%.

Small caps are particularly sensitive to interest rates because many smaller companies rely more heavily on borrowing and refinancing than highly profitable mega-cap companies.

That makes the Russell's underperformance worth watching.

Higher Treasury yields can also pressure expensive growth stocks because investors discount their future earnings at a higher rate.

This creates a major question for the market:

Can earnings growth remain strong enough to offset a higher interest-rate environment?

For now, investors have not abandoned equities. Friday's rebound showed that buyers are still willing to step in when inflation fears ease even slightly.

However, the market is becoming increasingly dependent on what happens in bonds and oil.

sections.heading: 2. Inflation: The Fed's Problem Is Not Going Away
body:
August inflation data gave the Federal Reserve another reason to remain cautious.

Consumer prices rose 0.4% month over month in August and 3.4% from a year earlier.

Core CPI, which removes food and energy, increased 0.3% during the month and 2.4% year over year.

Producer inflation was even stronger.

The Producer Price Index rose 0.4% in August and 5.4% compared with a year earlier.

One major reason for the increase was energy. Producer energy prices climbed 4.2% during August.

This matters because energy inflation can eventually spread through the economy.

Higher oil prices increase transportation costs.

Higher transportation costs increase the cost of moving products.

Businesses then have to decide whether to absorb those costs or pass them on to consumers.

That is why the recent oil move matters far beyond energy stocks.

sections.heading: 3. Oil Becomes the Market's Biggest Wild Card
body:
Energy was arguably the most important market story this week.

Brent crude finished Friday at $104.61 per barrel while WTI closed at $100.05.

Even after Friday's decline, crude gained more than 8% during the week.

Supply disruptions and escalating tensions around major Middle Eastern shipping routes have created renewed concerns about how much oil can reach global markets.

Shipping costs have also increased substantially.

The International Energy Agency now expects global oil supply to decline more sharply than previously forecast in 2026 as Gulf flows remain disrupted.

That creates an uncomfortable situation for central banks.

Normally, weaker economic activity might justify lower interest rates.

But if oil continues pushing inflation higher, central banks have less freedom to cut rates.

For investors, oil may therefore be just as important to watch as the next CPI report.

If crude falls back below $100, some inflation pressure could ease.

If it moves materially higher, markets could begin pricing in a longer period of restrictive monetary policy.

sections.heading: 4. Bonds: The 5% Question
body:
One of the most important numbers in the market right now is not the S&P 500.

It is the 10-year Treasury yield.

The yield ended the week around 4.97%, putting it extremely close to 5%.

That matters for several reasons.

First, Treasury securities become more attractive when investors can earn roughly 5% with substantially less risk than equities.

Second, higher yields increase borrowing costs across the economy, including mortgages, corporate debt, and business investment.

Third, higher yields reduce the present value investors are willing to assign to future corporate earnings.

That is especially important for technology and other high-growth companies whose valuations depend heavily on profits expected many years into the future.

A sustained move above 5% could therefore become a meaningful test for equity valuations.

sections.heading: 5. Earnings: AI Spending Is Still Producing Growth
body:
The macro environment dominated this week, but corporate earnings still gave investors important information.

Oracle

Oracle reported revenue of approximately $19.3 billion, up about 30% year over year.

Its revenue backlog reached roughly $664 billion as demand for AI cloud infrastructure continued expanding.

Oracle also signed more than $30 billion of new AI cloud contracts during the quarter.

The results helped demonstrate that large-scale corporate spending on AI infrastructure is still translating into real revenue growth.

However, Oracle's enormous capital spending remains an important risk. Investors continue to debate whether the long-term returns from AI infrastructure will justify the amount of capital being invested today.

Adobe

Adobe reported third-quarter revenue of $6.76 billion, ahead of Wall Street expectations.

Adjusted earnings were $6.13 per share.

AI-first annual recurring revenue increased more than 150% year over year, showing that Adobe is successfully generating demand for its new AI-based products.

However, investors remained cautious after the company's fourth-quarter revenue outlook came in slightly below expectations.

Together, Oracle and Adobe show the two sides of the current AI trade.

Demand is real and growing quickly.

But investors are becoming more demanding about profitability, monetization, and returns on AI investment

sections.heading: 6. The Consumer Is Starting to Matter More
body:
Another development worth watching is the consumer.

University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 47.8 in early September from 51.7 in August.

Consumers' one-year inflation expectations also jumped to 4.6%.

At the same time, weekly jobless claims remained low at 206,000, suggesting that employers are still not laying off workers aggressively.

That creates a mixed picture.

The labor market remains relatively stable, but consumers are becoming increasingly worried about prices.

Retailers are beginning to see some evidence of that pressure.

Kroger lowered its full-year comparable-sales outlook as shoppers became more cautious and inflation continued affecting purchasing behavior.

The strength of consumer spending will therefore be another major variable heading into the final months of 2026.

### 1. Federal Reserve Decision — September 16

This is the biggest event.

The Federal Reserve concludes its two-day meeting Wednesday and releases its interest-rate decision at 2:00 PM ET.

The Fed will also release updated economic projections.

Markets have moved toward expecting another rate increase after the latest inflation reports and surge in energy prices.

The most important part may not be the rate decision itself.

Investors will be watching the Fed's guidance on whether additional rate increases could follow.

### 2. August Retail Sales — September 16

Retail sales are released Wednesday morning at 8:30 AM ET.

This report will help show whether consumers are continuing to spend despite higher gasoline prices and weaker sentiment.

Strong sales combined with persistent inflation could strengthen the case for tighter monetary policy.

Weak sales could increase concerns that higher rates are beginning to slow the economy.

### 3. The 10-Year Treasury Yield

The 5% level is now extremely important.

A sustained break above it could create additional pressure on equity valuations.

A decline back toward 4.7%-4.8% would likely give growth stocks some relief.

### 4. Oil

WTI above $100 means energy is once again a meaningful inflation problem.

Any major change in Middle East supply conditions could quickly move both oil and bond markets.

### 5. AI Stocks

Oracle and Adobe showed that AI demand remains strong.

But the market is increasingly separating companies that can demonstrate real revenue and cash flow from companies trading primarily on AI expectations.

That distinction should become even more important going forward.

---

## Bottom Line

This week changed the market's risk equation.

Stocks remain near historically strong levels and corporate earnings continue to provide support, particularly in technology and AI.

But investors now have to deal with $100 oil, a 10-year Treasury yield near 5%, and inflation that is proving difficult to eliminate.

That combination makes the Federal Reserve the key catalyst heading into next week.

sections.heading: 7. What I'm Watching Next Week

quickTake:
This week's market was less about corporate earnings and more about a major shift in the macro environment.

Three forces are now interacting:

1. Oil prices above $100 are increasing inflation pressure.
2. Treasury yields are approaching levels that make bonds increasingly competitive with stocks.
3. The Federal Reserve may need to keep monetary policy tighter than investors expected.

That does not automatically mean the equity rally is finished.

It does mean that the conditions supporting higher valuations are becoming more difficult.

For investors, the September 16 Federal Reserve meeting could be one of the most important market events of the fall.
